I was unable to fetch the Ellicott page or get additional searches for Lutheran/Orthodox/NET Bible notes due to tool limits. However, I gathered substantial material from multiple traditions. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## 1 Samuel 28 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — Achish Drafts David
- **The setting:** "In those days" means while David dwelt at Ziklag. The Philistines are launching a large-scale war against Israel, larger than any since the valley of Elah. Achish, believing David has been raiding Israelite towns and is now his loyal vassal, tells David he must join the Philistine campaign. (Pulpit Commentary)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/28.htm
- **David's dilemma:** David is now caught "between a rock and a hard place." If he fights with the Philistines, he fights his own people and potentially kills Saul (whom he has sworn not to touch as the LORD's anointed). If he refuses, his 16-month deception collapses and Achish may destroy him. (Precept Austin)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-28-commentary
- **Clarke:** Achish issued this command because he was "deceived by what David had told him" about raiding Judah. (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html
- **Gill:** Achish was probably the head of the combined Philistine armies. David was in a "trying" situation — either fight his own countrymen (which his conscience could not allow) or be guilty of ingratitude to Achish and face severe consequences. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm

### v. 2 — David's Ambiguous Reply
- **David's words are deliberately ambiguous:** "You shall know what your servant can do" — Achish takes this as a boastful promise of valour, but David's real meaning may have been left deliberately vague. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew literally reads "knowing thou shalt know" — a strong affirmation, but David's reply is "really ambiguous." (Pulpit)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Gill:** David was "quite undetermined, and at a loss what to do, hoping that God in his providence would extricate him." Achish took the reply as hearty agreement and made David captain of his bodyguard for life. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Achish promoted David to "keeper of my head" — bodyguard for life. This is tragically ironic since David had already beheaded one Philistine giant (Goliath). (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Clarke:** David's reply "could only be understood by his succeeding conduct. It might imply what he could do in favour of the Philistines against Israel; or in favour of Israel against the Philistines." (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html

### v. 3 — Samuel's Death and Saul's Reform
- **Samuel's death repeated:** First reported in 1 Samuel 25:1, now mentioned again to "emphasize the spiritual vacuum left by Samuel's departure" and to explain Saul's desperate conduct that follows. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Saul had removed mediums and spiritists:** To his credit, Saul obeyed the Mosaic Law (Lev 19:31; 20:6, 27; Deut 18:9-14). This was likely done in his earlier days when still under Samuel's influence. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Gill adds:** Saul may have done this at Samuel's instigation, or from a superstitious fear that the evil spirit troubling him came from them — or to make "some appearance of zeal for religion." The fact is noted here to show Saul's "inconstancy" and folly in now seeking one out. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Saul's witch hunt was "one of the more Biblical actions he took in his 40-year reign. But it will also prove to be one of the most ironic acts of Saul, for he will seek that which he removed." (Precept Austin)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-28-commentary

### v. 4 — Battle Lines Drawn
- **Geography:** Shunem was in the territory of Issachar (Josh 19:18), in the valley of Jezreel (Esdraelon), on the slopes of Little Hermon, opposite Mount Gilboa. The Philistines had penetrated far north — about 20 miles north of Aphek, their most northerly city — showing their dominance over Saul's kingdom. (Pulpit)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Enduring Word:** "The geography of Shunem means that the Philistines made an aggressive attack against Saul and Israel." This was not a border raid but an invasion into the heartland. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Precept Austin:** Endor was about 2 miles north of Shunem and 6 miles north of Gilboa, meaning Saul would have to cross enemy territory to reach the medium — explaining his need for disguise. (Precept Austin)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-28-commentary

### v. 5 — Saul's Fear
- **Saul was afraid, his heart trembled greatly:** Long before his downward spiral, when Saul walked in the Spirit, he was a man of great courage (1 Sam 11:6-11). Saul began losing his courage when the Spirit withdrew (1 Sam 16:14); now after Samuel's death, it is almost completely gone. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Gill:** Saul feared because of the enemy's numbers, the death of Samuel, the loss of David (who might now fight against him), and his own guilty conscience — "he might fear the Lord would now reckon with him." (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Precept Austin contrasts Saul and David:** "Saul saw a giant force preparing to attack and feared because God had rejected him and was not with him. David saw a giant Philistine ready to attack but was not afraid because he came in the Name of the LORD of hosts." Two anointed kings, two giant enemies, two different hearts, two dramatically different outcomes. (Precept Austin)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-28-commentary
- **Clarke:** Saul saw "from the superiority of his enemies, from the state of his army, and especially from his own state towards God, that he had every thing to fear." (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html

### v. 6 — God's Silence
- **Three rejected channels:** Saul sought God through dreams, Urim, and prophets — the three standard means of divine guidance in Israel. All were silent. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Why God was silent:** "This silence demonstrates that God will not always answer everyone who seeks Him; not when a man is in a place of judgment as Saul is. King Saul has rejected and is currently rejecting God's previously revealed will." Saul knew God did not want him hunting David (1 Sam 24:16-20; 26:21), yet he disregarded that. If we want God to guide us, we must follow what we already know. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Constable (Evangelical):** "Since Saul had refused to listen to God in the past (chs. 13 and 15), God now refused to listen to him." Also notes that Abiathar the priest had taken the Urim and Thummim to David (1 Sam 22:20; 23:6-12), so Saul no longer had access to it. (Constable)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-28.html
- **Gill:** Saul's inquiry was not done "truly and heartily." The Urim was unavailable because Abiathar had fled with the ephod to David. As for prophets, a school existed at Naioth in Ramah, but God would not answer through them either. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Notes that 1 Chronicles 10:14 says Saul "did not inquire of the LORD" — the Hebrew verb *darash* there means a deep, earnest seeking after God Himself, not merely asking for an answer. Saul wanted information from God but "was not really seeking after God Himself." (Precept Austin)
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-28-commentary

### v. 7 — Saul Seeks a Medium
- **Desperation:** Saul's servants knew exactly where to find a medium — at Endor, despite Saul's own purge. The Hebrew word for medium (*owb*) has the idea of "mumbling" or speaking with a strange hollow sound — as if channeling. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Clarke:** "Strange that a man, who had banished all such from the land, as dangerous to the state, as impostors and deceivers, should now have recourse to them as the only persons in whom he could safely put his confidence in the time in which Jehovah had refused to help him!" (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html
- **Gill:** He sought a woman specifically because women were "most addicted to those wicked arts" and more easily imposed upon by Satan. "Saul showed himself to be as weak, to seek after such persons; but being left of God, he acted the part of a mad man, as well as of a bad man." (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Lange:** Endor was on the northern slope of Little Hermon, about 12 miles north of Gilboa. It is still marked by "a spring and numerous caves fit for the abode of witches." (Lange, cited at StudyLight)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/1-samuel-28.html

### v. 8 — Saul's Disguise and Journey
- **Disguised and at night:** Saul changed his royal robes and went under cover of darkness — a "work of darkness" in more ways than one. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **God's curse:** By consulting a medium, Saul brought upon himself the curse of Leviticus 20:6 — "I will set My face against that person and cut him off from his people." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Clarke:** He disguised himself so the woman would not be terrified and refuse her art. (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html

### v. 9 — The Woman's Suspicion
- **She fears a trap:** The woman suspected a government "sting" operation — she knew full well that Saul had been executing mediums. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Gill:** By her words, it is clear Saul did not merely expel mediums but put them to death, in accordance with Exodus 22:18. Saul hearing this "to his face must fill him with shame and confusion." (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm

### v. 10 — Saul's Oath
- **Swearing by the LORD in sin:** This is the last time Saul uses the name of the LORD in 1 Samuel — and he uses it to swear to a medium that she will not be punished. "Spiritual jargon means nothing." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Gill:** "It is much that Saul, being about such a work of darkness and wickedness, could take the name of the Lord into his mouth." Though he could shield her from civil punishment as king, "he could not secure her from eternal punishment." (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Constable:** "Saul sank so low as to swear to the woman in the Lord's name that he would not punish her for breaking the Lord's Law. This too was hypocrisy." (Constable)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-28.html

### v. 11 — "Bring Up Samuel"
- **Why Samuel?** Probably Saul wanted to remember his "good old days" with Samuel, when the prophet was his guide and mentor (1 Sam 9:25-26). Saul forgot that Samuel was in fact his adversary when he slipped into sin. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Gill:** "It argued extreme folly and madness in him to imagine, that the spirit of this great and good man was at the beck of a witch." (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Clarke:** The woman "certainly meant no more than making her familiar personify whomsoever the querist should wish." She had no power over actual departed human souls. (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html

### v. 12 — The Woman's Shock
- **She cries out:** The medium was probably a fraud whose dealings with the spirit realm were mere tricks; now something real happened and she was completely surprised. Also, she now recognized Saul and realized her life was in danger. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Three main views on what happened here (summarizing multiple sources):**

  **View 1 — It really was Samuel, by God's permission.** This is held by Enduring Word (Guzik), Clarke, Ellicott (cited in the search excerpts), the Haydock Catholic Commentary, and Constable. The medium had no power over Samuel; God sent him for a special purpose — to confirm the coming judgment. Guzik compares this to Moses and Elijah appearing at the Transfiguration (Matt 17:3). Clarke: "I believe that the woman of En-dor had no power over Samuel… Samuel really came, but not because the medium called for him. Samuel appeared because God had a special purpose for it."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html

  **View 2 — It was a demonic impersonation.** Gill holds this view firmly: the true Samuel's soul was at rest in Abraham's bosom, and "it was not in the power of men and devils to disquiet it." A demon appeared in Samuel's form. Gill also argues the true Samuel would not have admitted being "brought up" (he would have said "come down" from heaven) and would not have accepted homage from Saul. Gill calls it a "diabolical spectre."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm

  **View 3 — It was deception by the woman (ventriloquism/clairvoyance).** Dummelow says the woman was a "medium" in the modern sense, and "very possibly Saul saw nothing at all; the words he heard may have come from the woman." The Septuagint translators used the word *engastrimuthos* (ventriloquist). Whedon's Commentary develops a clairvoyant hypothesis — the woman could "place herself in mesmeric intercourse with the souls of those who came to inquire of her" and read Saul's own mind, then pretended to be Samuel.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/1-samuel-28.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/1-samuel-28.html

- **Catholic view (Haydock):** "It is the more common opinion of the holy fathers, and interpreters, that the soul of Samuel appeared indeed… Not that the power of her magic could bring him thither, but that God was pleased for the punishment of Saul, that Samuel himself should denounce unto him the evils that were falling upon him." Cites Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 46:23 as decisive: "he slept and he made known to the king, and showed him the end of his life, and he lifted up his voice from the earth, in prophecy."
  — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/1_samuel/28.htm

- **Reformed/Presbyterian (Dale Ralph Davis, The Gospel Coalition):** Davis says the question probably cannot be resolved. "Is the spirit the medium summons actually Samuel? Apparently so, since what 'Samuel' says in vv. 16-19 is entirely consistent with what he had said prior to his death." He focuses on the theological message rather than resolving the mechanics: "Don't try to tidy things up with queries about whether Saul was 'really saved.'… The last time we see Saul here, he is walking out into the night (v. 25), cut off from God and his Word. It's meant to be scary."
  — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/you-asked-how-do-you-explain-the-witch-from-endor/

### v. 13 — "I See a God (Elohim) Coming Up"
- **The word *elohim*:** The medium used the Hebrew word *elohim* (literally "gods"), but speaking from her pagan context, she did not mean the One True God nor that Samuel was deified. It was simply her pagan vocabulary for a majestic, supernatural being. The Targum renders it "an angel of the Lord." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Clarke:** "This sight alarmed the woman; it was what she did not expect; in this she could not recognise her familiar, and she was terrified at the appearance." (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html
- **Constable:** The term *elohim* also describes judges in Israel (Ps 82:6; cf. John 10:35). "Perhaps the woman meant that the man she saw looked like a judge or like a divine being because he was imposing." (Constable)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-28.html

### v. 14 — The Mantle and Recognition
- **"An old man… covered with a mantle":** The mantle (Hebrew *meheel*, robe) is significant. In 1 Samuel 15:27, when Samuel announced God's rejection of Saul, Saul grabbed Samuel's robe (*meheel*) and tore it. Samuel then said, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today." It is likely Samuel appeared wearing this same torn robe, reminding Saul that the kingdom was torn from him. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Saul bowed:** This is hypocritical homage — Saul had not previously obeyed Samuel, nor was he about to act on the warning he would receive. (Constable)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-28.html
- **Gill disagrees that Saul bowed to Samuel at all:** Some Jewish interpreters, noted by Gill, think the text describes *Samuel* bowing to *Saul* out of reverence for him as king, though Gill himself dismisses this. (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm

### v. 15 — Samuel's Complaint and Saul's Plea
- **"Why have you disturbed me?":** Samuel's words indicate he was in a place of rest and had no wish to return to the "fret and fever of this life." (Ellicott, as quoted in search results)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/28.htm
- **Enduring Word notes on the afterlife:** Samuel was not in heaven proper but in "Abraham's bosom" — the place of comfort for the believing dead before Christ's finished work opened heaven. This is based on Jesus' teaching in Luke 16:19-31. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Saul's threefold distress:** (1) The Philistines are warring against him. (2) God has departed from him. (3) God no longer answers him. The second is far worse than the first. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **"What I should do":** Baldwin (quoted by Guzik) says: "Saul is asking for guidance when his course of action is obvious: he has to fight the Philistines. What he really wants is reassurance that all will be well and that he will win the battle." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Gill (from the demonic-impersonation view):** The complaint "Why hast thou disquieted me?" proves this wasn't the real Samuel — the true Samuel's soul was at rest and it was not in the power of men or devils to disquiet it. Also, a real Samuel would have said "come down" not "brought up." (Gill)
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm

### v. 16 — "Why Do You Ask Me?"
- **Samuel reasons:** If the LORD has departed from Saul and become his enemy, what use is it asking Samuel? Samuel was on the LORD's side. Saul kept seeking, hoping the news would get better — but it never did. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Clarke:** The meaning is: "Was ever I wont to give answers that were not dictated by the Lord? It is his counsel alone that I communicate." (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html
- **Constable:** "Samuel replied that Saul was wrong in thinking that Samuel would tell him what strategy to use since the Lord would not. The prophet was, after all, simply the mouthpiece of God." (Constable)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-28.html

### vv. 17-18 — The Unchanged Verdict
- **The message is exactly the same as 15:28:** Samuel quotes his own earlier words — "the LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David." About fifteen years had passed since 1 Samuel 15, but God had not changed His mind. "Perhaps Saul thought that time would change God's mind, but time never changes God's mind." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **The specific sin:** Saul's failure to execute God's fierce wrath against Amalek (1 Samuel 15). That original disobedience was the decisive turning point. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **The test of any "spirit encounter":** "Even if an angel from heaven (or Samuel himself!) preach any other gospel to you… let him be accursed" (Gal 1:8). The test is faithfulness to the already-revealed Biblical message. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/

### v. 19 — "Tomorrow You and Your Sons Will Be with Me"
- **The death sentence:** Samuel tells Saul he will die the next day. He never told Saul *what to do* because it was too late — only what would happen. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **"With me" does not necessarily mean heaven:** In the Old Testament understanding of Sheol, both the blessed and cursed dead were in the same general realm but separated (as in Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus, Luke 16:19-31). Samuel was in the place of comfort; Saul would not be. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Clarke's pastoral note:** "Can any person read this, properly considering the situation of this unfortunate monarch, the triumph of the enemies of God, and the speedy ruin in which the godlike Jonathan is about to be involved, without feeling the keenest anguish of heart?" Clarke also quotes Charles Wesley's poetic paraphrase: "What do these solemn words portend? A ray of hope when life shall end. Thou and thy sons, though slain, shall be To-morrow in repose with me." Clarke adds: "Saul had committed the sin unto death — the sin to be visited with a violent death, while the mercy of God was extended to the soul." (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html
- **Davis (Reformed):** "'You and your sons will be with me' does not mean that Saul was going to heaven… He is making no assessment or statement about Saul's eternal state here." (The Gospel Coalition)
  — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/you-asked-how-do-you-explain-the-witch-from-endor/

### v. 20 — Saul Collapses
- **Saul fell full length:** He was so overwhelmed that he swooned, falling at his own length on the ground. He had eaten nothing all day and all night. (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html
- **The worst part:** It wasn't just the news of his death. "Far worse to Saul was the knowledge that the LORD was his adversary. Not only were the Philistines set against him, so was the LORD God." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/

### vv. 21-22 — The Medium's Compassion
- **A tragic irony:** The medium — a practitioner of forbidden arts — comforts the king of Israel. "It's a sad note when a practitioner of the occult comforts the king of Israel. But they were two of the same kind; each lived in rebellion against God." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Constable notes a literary parallel:** The woman's words echo Samuel's. Samuel said: because you did not obey God, God has done this to you (v. 18). The woman says: because I obeyed you, you should now obey me and eat (vv. 21-22). "Saul realizes he has landed in a situation which resembles a covenant with the medium instead of with YHWH." (Constable, citing Beuken)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-28.html
- **"A morsel of bread":** The woman offers Saul food so he can have strength for his journey back — a last act of human kindness before his death. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/

### vv. 23-24 — The Meal
- **Saul initially refuses** but his servants and the woman together urge him until he relents. (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Fatted calf and unleavened bread:** The fatted calf was kept ready for immediate slaughter (common in hot climates where meat could not be stored). Unleavened bread was used because there was no time for dough to rise — everything was done in haste. (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html
- **The meal as last supper:** "The dinner Saul ate that night was like the last meal of a man on death row, awaiting execution in the morning." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/

### v. 25 — Departure into Darkness
- **"They rose and went away that night":** The entire chapter's events occur in a single night. Saul left "resigned to his sad and tragic fate." (Enduring Word)
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/
- **Davis (Reformed) closes with a pastoral warning:** "The last time we see Saul here, he is walking out into the night (v. 25), cut off from God and his Word. It's meant to be scary; that's not necessarily bad — 'twas grace that taught my heart to fear." (The Gospel Coalition)
  — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/you-asked-how-do-you-explain-the-witch-from-endor/
- **Clarke:** "The next day, in all probability, the battle happened in which Israel was defeated, and Saul and his sons lost their lives." All the transactions of this chapter — arrival, consultation, the meal, departure — occupy one night only. (Clarke)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences

### The Nature of the Apparition — The Main Dividing Point

| Tradition | View | Representative Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik) | The real Samuel appeared, sent by God, not by the medium's power. The medium was terrified because she encountered the genuine supernatural. | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-28/ |
| **Older Baptist** (Gill) | A demonic impersonation. The true Samuel could not be disturbed by witchcraft; Satan mimicked him. | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/28.htm |
| **Methodist/Wesleyan** (Clarke) | The real Samuel appeared, sent by God's mercy. The medium's arts had no effect; Samuel came independently to warn Saul. | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-samuel-28.html |
| **Methodist/Wesleyan** (Whedon) | A clairvoyant reading. The woman read Saul's own thoughts and fears; no actual spirit appeared. | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/1-samuel-28.html |
| **Reformed/Presbyterian** (Dale Ralph Davis / TGC) | "Apparently" the real Samuel, based on consistency with his prior words. But the mechanics are deliberately under-described. The theological message matters more. | https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/you-asked-how-do-you-explain-the-witch-from-endor/ |
| **Catholic** (Haydock) | Samuel's soul really appeared, by God's permission, as affirmed by the Fathers (Justin Martyr, Origen, Ambrose, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, Theodoret) and Sirach 46:23. | https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/1_samuel/28.htm |
| **Evangelical** (Constable) | God allowed Samuel (or a vision of him) to appear — the last divine revelation Saul received. A demon could not have spoken the truth of vv. 16-19. | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-28.html |

### Other Distinctive Emphases
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Guzik): Emphasises the reality of the spirit world, the danger of occult practices today (tarot, Ouija boards, horoscopes), and God's ability to speak through unusual means.
- **Reformed** (Davis): Emphasises the sovereignty of God in judgment, the finality of Saul's rejection, and the pastoral "fear" the text should produce — warning against treating God's silence lightly.
- **Catholic** (Haydock): Emphasises the patristic consensus that Samuel truly appeared, and the passage as evidence for the afterlife and the intercession/witness of the saints.
- **Older Baptist** (Gill): Strongest emphasis on the impossibility of a witch having power over a saint, leading to the demonic-impersonation view. Gill also uniquely notes the Jewish tradition that this woman was Abner's mother.
